tweets.text:
$HG $HGRAF #Graphene #Nanotechnology

Imagine waking up in 2035.

You pick up your phone. It contains fractal graphene.

You get into your EV. Fractal graphene.

The tires, battery components, lubricants and lightweight composites? Fractal graphene.

Even the graphene-enhanced asphalt beneath the car could be stronger, longer-lasting and more resistant to cracking.

The airplane you board. The data center powering AI. Wind turbines. Medical devices. Concrete. Coatings. Packaging. Water filtration. Sporting goods. Electronics. Aerospace. Defense.

Fractal graphene is everywhere.

Not because companies wanted “graphene.”

Because they wanted products that are lighter, stronger, more conductive, more durable and more sustainable.

If HydroGraph’s production process continues to prove scalable, cost-effective and consistent, the opportunity is not about replacing one material in one industry.

It is about becoming an enabling material across dozens of trillion-dollar industries.

I am not saying this future is guaranteed.

I am saying that if fractal graphene becomes a standard performance additive, today’s valuation could one day look astonishingly small.

Sometimes the biggest winners are not the companies selling the finished product.

They are the ones supplying the material inside millions—or even billions—of products.

This new paper argues that many docking models perform well on familiar targets but struggle on truly novel ones. The authors propose a hybrid physics + AI approach and back it with prospective wet-lab validation.

If these results hold up, this could represent an important step toward making AI a more reliable engine for discovering new medicines.

DeFi will become far more important than most people realise. And not because more people start using it. Because the users stop being people at all.

When you think about it DeFi is actually better suited to machines than it is to us. An agent doesn't need a website, or buttons, or a front end. You can strip all of it away and just let the agent plug straight into the protocol, do the job, and leave.

Now play it forward… An AI agent taking out a flash loan at 3 am, another paying half a cent for a bit of data to a different agent, and one moving its treasury across three chains in a second because a swap suddenly got cheaper somewhere.

Genuinely hard to wrap your head around… but this is the user base DeFi ends up serving.

This is the Economic Singularity I've been telling you about at the ground level, where the financial system is being rebuilt for users with no faces, no emotions, and no need for downtime.

tweets.text: You're right. I look at dishonesty as a reality to deal with well, rather than a moral issue; though, it is of course a moral issue. In other words, I treat dishonesty as a structural issue. When people lie, I look at the severity, context, and patterns to decide whether they’re fundamentally honest but imperfect or habitually dishonest. It tells me about the person and how to deal with them. The goal is to align incentives with integrity so that truth‑telling becomes the rational choice, while still being practical—because if I only worked with perfect people, I’d have no one. However, with most dishonest people that won't work so I avoid them.

TL;DR

- The bottleneck for AI is no longer money—it’s power. Capital is abundant, but electricity, transformers, GPUs, cooling, networking and data centres are the scarce resources limiting AI growth. 

- Energy and AI can both be broken into four layers: Make, Move, Store, Sell. This framework helps identify where value will accrue across the stack. 

- For electricity, these correspond to generating power, transmitting it, storing it (batteries/thermal storage), and selling it through utilities and power markets. 

- For AI, they correspond to creating models and chips, networking and interconnects, memory and context storage, and finally applications and APIs that sell intelligence. 

-We are at an inflection point because AI demand has exploded, energy technologies (especially solar and batteries) have become economically viable, governments now view AI and energy as strategic priorities, and a new generation of founders has emerged to build hard-tech companies. 

- The biggest long-term winners will be systems companies that vertically integrate hardware, software, energy and operations rather than pure software businesses. 

- Today’s infrastructure bottlenecks - GPUs, transformers, cooling, networking and power equipment - are tomorrow’s platforms. The biggest companies will emerge by solving these constraints, not simply exploiting them temporarily. 

- Compute factories (next-generation AI data centres) are becoming the “refineries” of the AI era, manufacturing intelligence by integrating power, cooling, networking, chips and software into one system. 

- AI is accelerating an enormous buildout across energy infrastructure, batteries, compute markets and frontier power technologies (SMRs, geothermal, fusion, etc.), compressing decades of learning into just a few years.

- The core investment thesis is simple: intelligence is humanity’s highest-return asset, so the biggest opportunities lie in companies that lower the cost of producing intelligence - or the energy required to create it.
